title: Assertion `(expected_utf16_length) == (utf16_length)' failed
body: I am using Node.js v19.8.1 on Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.22621.0 x64. In the Node CLI, every time I start typing `new Date`, the CLI closes with an assertion failure in `c:\ws\src\inspector\node_string.cc`: `(expected_utf16_length) == (utf16_length)`. I expect `new Date()` to display the current date.

symptoms_visible: In Node.js v19.8.1 on Windows 11 x64, the REPL closes every time I start typing `new Date`, with an assertion that expected_utf16_length equals utf16_length.
N0.label: N0 Windows REPL assertion reported

symptoms_visible: The crash occurs before I can finish typing the command in v19.8.1.
The same date expression works when I enter it inside `console.log`, and `new Date()` works normally in v19.6.1.
N1.label: N1 version and expression behavior compared

symptoms_visible: The REPL crashes under PowerShell, Command Prompt, and Git Bash on native Windows.
Node.js v19.8.1 accepts `new Date()` normally inside Ubuntu on WSL2.
N2.label: N2 native Windows scope established

symptoms_visible: Affected Windows release binaries across Node 18, 19, and 20 can abort while text is typed directly into the REPL.
Some non-ASCII input also triggers a string-length assertion in the REPL, while executing a script is fine.
An official Windows binary reproduces the abort, but a locally compiled Visual Studio 2022 build does not.
N3.label: N3 release-build-specific REPL pattern identified

symptoms_visible: A Windows x64 release-mode CI build made with Visual Studio 2019 consistently aborts in the REPL history navigation test with a related UTF string-length assertion.
The failure can be reproduced with the icelake processing path under Visual Studio 2019, while other tested build combinations do not show it.
N4.label: N4 compiler and CPU-path interaction reproduced

symptoms_visible: With the candidate dependency change applied to the Visual Studio 2019 Node build, the previously failing REPL history navigation test passes.
I have not retested an official Windows release containing that change on the original affected machine.
N5.label: N5 candidate change verified in CI build

symptoms_visible: A maintainer reports that the dependency update containing the workaround has been pushed for future Node releases; I have not yet retested an official fixed Windows release on the original affected system.
N_terminal.label: terminal fix landed but reporter has not retested

question_patterns: Can you test the same REPL command with Node.js v19.6.1 and report what happens?
Does an older Node 19 build reproduce the assertion?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: There is no error in v19.6.1. `new Date()` returns `2023-04-07T14:00:29.886Z` normally.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The same assertion occurs in v19.6.1 and every older Node version I tried.
It works in v19.6.1, but the timestamp is different because I tested later.

question_patterns: Does it crash after you submit the expression, or while you are still typing it?
Can you show exactly when the REPL closes?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: It does not even let me finish the command. The REPL closes while I am typing `new Date`; I attached a screenshot.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: It only crashes after I press Enter and Node evaluates the completed expression.

question_patterns: Does the same expression work when it is nested inside another call?
What happens if you enter `console.log(new Date())`?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: There is no problem if I call it inside a function. `console.log(new Date())` prints the date and then `undefined`.

edges.comment: Reporter messages c1 and c5: the older-version probe is clean, and the reporter clarifies that the failure occurs during REPL typing rather than Date evaluation. The screenshot is the reporter's c5 attachment.

question_patterns: Does the problem persist in a different native Windows terminal?
Please try the Node REPL from Command Prompt, PowerShell, or another terminal and tell me whether any of them behave differently.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Yes, it persists in all the native Windows terminals I have installed. I tried Command Prompt, Git Bash, and PowerShell.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: It only happens in one third-party terminal; Command Prompt and PowerShell both work.
It reproduces in Command Prompt and PowerShell, but I do not have Git Bash installed.

question_patterns: Can you test the same Node version in WSL and report whether the REPL crashes there?
Does the behavior persist outside the native Windows build?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: It works in Ubuntu on WSL2. With Node.js v19.8.1 there, `new Date()` returns a timestamp normally.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The same Node version crashes in WSL2 with the same assertion.

edges.comment: Reporter messages c13-c14: switching native terminal applications does not change the result, while the Linux build inside WSL2 works. These are environment probes, not persistent fixes.

question_patterns: Which other Node release versions have shown the same Windows REPL failure?
Can anyone reproduce this on another supported Node line?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I have seen the same kind of failure in Windows release builds from Node 18, 19, and 20. Older builds such as 18.15.0 work, while affected examples include 18.16.x, 18.17.x, 19.8.1, and later Node 20 releases.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Only v19.8.1 is affected; every Node 18 and Node 20 release I tested works.

question_patterns: Can you try entering non-ASCII text directly into the REPL and paste the raw result?
Do other inputs trigger a similar assertion while typing?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Entering characters such as `é` directly in an affected Node REPL can also abort with a UTF string-length assertion. The exact result varies with the character; some supplementary characters do not crash when used as the first character.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: All non-ASCII input works normally; only the ASCII text `new Date` triggers the assertion.

question_patterns: Does the same input fail when executed from a script, or only while typing in the interactive shell?
Can you compare direct REPL input with running a file?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The problem only occurs while typing directly in the Node shell. Executing a script is fine.

question_patterns: Can you compare an official Windows binary with a locally compiled Node binary on the same type of system?
Does a local source build reproduce what the downloaded release build does?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The downloaded Windows release binary reproduces it. When I build current Node from source with Visual Studio 2022 and run that generated `node.exe`, I cannot reproduce the problem.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The official binary and my local source build both fail identically.
The official binary fails and two separate local Visual Studio 2022 builds both work.

edges.comment: Messages c15-c29 from several affected Windows users and a maintainer are folded into one simulated user side. This establishes recurrence across release lines, REPL-specific non-ASCII triggers, and the official-binary versus local-build difference without yet assigning a root cause.

question_patterns: Can you reproduce this in CI using a release-mode Windows build, and share the build command and raw failing test output?
Which compiler setup reproduces the assertion in an automated Node test?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Our Windows x64 CI consistently fails `test-repl-history-navigation.js` when built with the Visual Studio 2019 toolchain using approximately `.\vcbuild build-release nosign x64`. The stack reaches `StringUtil::StringViewToUtf8` and aborts because the expected and actual UTF-8 lengths differ.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The release-mode CI test passes under Visual Studio 2019, and I can reproduce the failure only in a debug build made with a different compiler.

question_patterns: What toolchain and command does the official Windows release job use?
How does the release build environment differ from the local build that works?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The official Windows release job uses Visual Studio 2019 and runs `vcbuild.bat build-release` with the target architecture and upload step. My non-reproducing local build used Visual Studio 2022.

question_patterns: Please run Coreinfo on the CI hardware and share the reported CPU feature lines.
What processor and instruction features does the reproducing machine report?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The machine has an 11th Gen Intel Core i7-1185G7. Coreinfo marks AVX-512-F, DQ, IFAMA, CD, BW, and VL as supported.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Coreinfo reports no AVX-512 support at all on the reproducing machine.

question_patterns: Can you force the available processing kernels under each compiler setup and report which combination reproduces the failure?
Please compare the same test across the available optimized and fallback paths.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The failure is reproducible on the icelake kernel when compiled with Visual Studio 2019. I do not reproduce it with my Visual Studio 2022 build.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Every optimized and fallback path fails under both Visual Studio 2019 and Visual Studio 2022.

edges.comment: Messages c30-c43: build-team and CI-operator evidence is folded into the user side. The answers preserve the raw build command, assertion location, CPU feature output, and kernel/compiler reproduction matrix; the causal interpretation remains engineer-side.

question_patterns: Can you rebuild Node with the candidate dependency change and rerun the previously failing test?
Please test the proposed library patch in the same Windows CI configuration and report only whether the reproducer and Node test still fail.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I applied the candidate upstream change, rebuilt Node with Visual Studio 2019, and the standalone test case was fixed. `test-repl-history-navigation.js` also passes again in that build.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The standalone reproducer and the Node REPL test still fail after applying the candidate dependency change.
The candidate change fixes the Node REPL test in two repeated Visual Studio 2019 CI runs.

edges.comment: Participant10's c43 pre-landing verification is folded into the user side as CI-operator evidence. It confirms the candidate change on the reproducing build, but it is not the original reporter retesting an official release.

solution.intent: Update Node's simdutf dependency so Windows binaries built with Visual Studio 2019 do not select the faulty icelake AVX-512 transcoding path, then ask affected users to verify an official build containing the change.
solution.concrete_example: Use the simdutf update that disables its icelake optimized path when compiled by Visual Studio 2019. Publish it in a future Windows Node build, then ask the original affected user to type the same REPL input in that official build and report whether the assertion is gone.
solution.inference_hint: The final maintainer diagnosis connects the raw matrix—official Visual Studio 2019 release builds fail, Visual Studio 2022 builds do not, the affected CPU supports AVX-512, and only the icelake path reproduces—to incorrect UTF-16/UTF-8 transcoding results from simdutf's optimized kernel. The selected workaround is to disable that kernel for Visual Studio 2019 builds.

edges.comment: Final accepted diagnosis from c39-c45: simdutf's icelake AVX-512 transcoding path produces incorrect results in Visual Studio 2019 release builds. The dependency update was pushed and passed participant10's CI test, but the original reporter never confirmed an official fixed release; terminal resolution therefore remains unverified.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the final accepted root cause: the Windows release build's simdutf icelake AVX-512 transcoding path produces incorrect UTF conversion results when compiled in release mode with Visual Studio 2019.

The diagnosis must be grounded in the collected evidence: affected official binaries versus a working Visual Studio 2022 source build, the Visual Studio 2019 CI reproducer, CPU feature output, the kernel/compiler reproduction matrix, and the passing candidate-change test.

Must recommend the simdutf update that disables the icelake optimized path for Visual Studio 2019 builds, rather than treating malformed user input, Date evaluation, or a particular terminal application as the root cause.

Must not present switching among native Windows terminals as a fix; Command Prompt, PowerShell, and Git Bash all reproduced the failure. WSL or downgrading may avoid it but do not repair the affected Windows release build.

Must ask an affected user to verify an official Node build containing the dependency fix before declaring the original report resolved; the thread only contains CI-operator verification of the candidate change.

persona_hint.experience_level: The opening reporter is an ordinary Node.js user who can compare versions and terminals. Later affected users, a build operator, and a CI engineer contribute increasingly technical Windows build, CPU-feature, and test evidence; these participants are folded into one simulated user side.
persona_hint.communication_style: Initially brief and practical, supplying exact commands, stack traces, and screenshots; later responses are technical and evidence-driven, with raw build commands, test output, and hardware details when specifically requested.
